intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Wolfram syndrome-2 (WFS2) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CISD2 gene (611507) on chromosome 4q24.

paragraphs.text: Wolfram syndrome-2 is an autosomal recessive disorder. Like Wolfram syndrome, it is defined by insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and optic atrophy. In the families in which it was first described, diabetes insipidus was absent and several patients had profound upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding (El-Shanti et al., 2000). Mozzillo et al. (2014) noted that WFS2 differs from WFS1 in that it lacks diabetes insipidus and psychiatric disorders and includes bleeding upper intestinal ulcers and defective platelet aggregation.

checks.claim: Wolfram syndrome-2 is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Wolfram syndrome, which is sometimes referred to as "DIDMOAD" (diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, and deafness), is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder
checks.explanation: The abstract calls Wolfram syndrome in general autosomal recessive. It does not say so specifically for the 4q-linked form, although homozygosity mapping implies recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: Like Wolfram syndrome, Wolfram syndrome-2 is defined by insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and optic atrophy.
checks.evidence_quote: for which only insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and optic atrophy are necessary to make the diagnosis
checks.explanation: This diagnostic definition is given for Wolfram syndrome in general. The abstract only says the 4q-linked patients 'have the Wolfram syndrome phenotype'.

checks.claim: In the families in which Wolfram syndrome-2 was first described, diabetes insipidus was absent.
checks.evidence_quote: There is an absence of diabetes insipidus in all affected family members.
checks.explanation: Diabetes insipidus was absent in all affected members of all four families, so it was also absent in the three 4q-linked families.

paragraphs.text: Mozzillo et al. (2014) described a Caucasian girl with WFS2. She was the first child of parents who said they were not consanguineous. From age 5 years she had recurrent bleeding upper intestinal ulcers. At 14 years she was diagnosed with malrotation and partial duodenal intussusception, and a duodenal segment was resected with duodenal-jejunal anastomosis. At 16 years she developed reduced visual acuity and dyschromatopsia. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left. Fundus examination showed optic disc pallor with preserved pupillary light reflexes bilaterally. Pattern VEPs were normal, and brain MRI showed normal optic nerve caliber. Nonautoimmune diabetes began at 17 years and was treated with insulin. She also had bilateral sensorineural hearing loss in the high frequencies, slow intestinal transit, and entero-gastric bile reflux. Her ocular findings were unchanged after 5 years of follow-up. Visual field testing, ERG, microperimetry, and OCT then showed moderate involvement of the optic nerve in both eyes, consistent with optic neuropathy, and excluded optic atrophy. At 22 years she had diabetes mellitus, optic neuropathy with preserved visual acuity and normal electrophysiologic tests, no optic atrophy, tinnitus, entero-gastric bile reflux, slow intestinal transit, and bleeding upper intestinal ulcers. Her parents and brother had no ophthalmologic abnormalities, diabetes, or deafness.

paragraphs.text: Mozzillo et al. (2014) found that their patient had a reduced, reversible platelet aggregation defect in response to ADP at concentrations up to 10 microM, and her platelets showed no secretion in response to ADP. Aggregation in response to collagen, epinephrine, and ristocetin was normal. Her bleeding score was 3 (normal 3 or less), and other main coagulation tests were normal. Her parents and brother were heterozygous carriers and also had a reversible platelet aggregation defect in response to ADP. The authors noted that Jordanian WFS2 patients had been described with defective aggregation to collagen rather than to ADP. Because collagen- and ADP-induced aggregation are both calcium-mediated, they suggested that differences in experimental conditions or variability between patients might explain the discrepancy.

paragraphs.text: El-Shanti et al. (2000) described Wolfram syndrome as an autosomal recessive disorder and mapped this form by homozygosity mapping. Amr et al. (2007) found a homozygous mutation in 3 consanguineous Jordanian families, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. In the patient reported by Mozzillo et al. (2014), the CISD2 deletion was homozygous, and her unaffected parents and brother were heterozygous. The parents reported that they were not consanguineous, but their grandparents had been born on the same small Italian island where the family still lived. Long runs of homozygosity in the SNP-array data showed no degree of parental relationship. However, microsatellite analysis supported a common ancestor.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 3 consanguineous families of Jordanian descent with WFS2, Amr et al. (2007) identified a homozygous missense mutation in the ZCD2 (CISD2) gene. The mutation was a G-to-C transversion at nucleotide 109 that predicted a glu37-to-gln (E37Q) substitution at a conserved residue. The families had been shown not to carry WFS1 mutations and had been mapped to the WFS2 locus. Although the change was nonsynonymous, Amr et al. (2007) concluded that it causes disease through aberrant splicing: it disrupted mRNA splicing by eliminating exon 2, which introduced a premature stop codon.

paragraphs.text: In a Caucasian girl with WFS2, Mozzillo et al. (2014) identified a novel homozygous intragenic deletion of the CISD2 gene that removed the whole of exon 2. PCR failed to amplify exon 2 in the patient, and cDNA sequencing showed the deletion. SNP-array analysis of the trio confirmed the deletion and showed that her parents and brother were heterozygous carriers. Combined with the PCR data, the array results restricted the maximum size of the deletion to 2,050 bp, spanning intron 2 to intron 3; the minimum size was 739 bp. The deleted region included the codons for amino acids WRSKT (residues 102 to 106), within the 2Fe-2S domain. The authors suggested that this may result in a nonfunctional protein.

paragraphs.text: Amr et al. (2007) showed that ERIS (endoplasmic reticulum intermembrane small protein), the protein encoded by ZCD2, localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum but does not interact directly with wolframin. When stimulated with thapsigargin, lymphoblastoid cells from affected individuals showed a significantly greater rise in intracellular calcium than control cells. Resting intracellular calcium concentrations did not differ.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2009) found that Cisd2 deficiency in mice caused mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction accompanied by autophagic cell death. These events preceded the 2 earliest signs of nerve and muscle degeneration, and together they produced a set of features suggestive of premature aging. Mitochondrial degeneration worsened with age, and autophagy increased in parallel with the development of the premature aging phenotype. The authors proposed the knockout mouse as an animal model for WFS2.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 3 consanguineous Jordanian families with Wolfram syndrome-2, Amr et al. (2007) identified a homozygous G-to-C transversion at nucleotide 109 of the ZCD2 (CISD2) gene, predicting a glu37-to-gln (E37Q) substitution at a conserved residue. The mutation disrupted mRNA splicing by eliminating exon 2, which introduced a premature stop codon. Amr et al. (2007) concluded that this aberrant splicing is the basis of pathogenesis.

paragraphs.text: In a Caucasian girl with Wolfram syndrome-2, Mozzillo et al. (2014) identified a homozygous intragenic deletion of the CISD2 gene that removed the whole of exon 2. The maximum size of the deletion was 2,050 bp, spanning intron 2 to intron 3. Her parents and brother were heterozygous carriers and had a subclinical reversible defect of platelet aggregation in response to ADP. The deleted region included the codons for residues 102 to 106 within the 2Fe-2S domain.
